title: Beyond and within

segments.voice: Yesterday, nirgun and its twin, sargun: the One beyond every quality and present in every form. Your line: vast and close.

Dusk, and in a temple in Guru Nanak's world, priests lift trays: little lamps, flowers, incense, a pearl or two, waved in circles before an image. It's called aarti, a worship of light. Tradition tells of Guru Nanak watching a ceremony like this, then stepping outside and singing his own. His tray was much bigger. You met that hymn in year two. Sikhs still sing it at the end of the day, and it holds today's idea, because in one hymn it goes as far out as a hymn can go, and then as far in.
screen: `LAMPS ON A TRAY, AT DUSK.` → `GURU NANAK SINGS HIS OWN.` → `AS FAR OUT, THEN AS FAR IN.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens, in paraphrase: the sky is the tray, the sun and moon are the lamps, the stars are the pearls. The breeze is the incense, the wind is the fan, and all the forests are flowers. The whole universe is already doing aarti, and no temple tray could hold it. That's beyond: the One past every size we can manage. The English word is transcendent. Then the hymn turns, again in paraphrase: in everything there is a light, and that light is You. By that light, everything is lit. Five days ago that line held the many sangats together. Here it sits where Guru Nanak placed it, right after the sky-sized tray, in Sohila, the bedtime prayer. That's within: the One inside every living thing. The English word is immanent. The turn is the point. Guru Nanak doesn't sing one hymn for the stars and another for the heart. He sings one, and you can't keep one half and drop the other. Look back at the week: many sangats under one Guru, many streams, many names, the name Waheguru, nirgun and sargun. Each day circled the same shape. Many, and one. This hymn says it under an open sky. Beyond and within.
screen: `THE SKY IS THE TRAY.` · `IN EVERYTHING, A LIGHT.` · `ONE HYMN, NOT TWO.` · `THE WEEK: MANY, AND ONE.` · then, large: `BEYOND AND WITHIN.`

segments.voice: Look up, out a window or in your mind: the sky as a tray, the sun or moon as a lamp, the moving air as incense, and let it be huge. Then close your eyes and turn the same attention inward, to the warmth of your own breath. Same attention, different direction.
Beyond and within. Transcendent and immanent at once: the One past every size, and the light inside every living thing, held in one hymn. Today's word.
Your line: beyond and within. One hymn, sung under the whole sky. That's the week.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite Sohila at night, which includes Guru Nanak's aarti picturing the sky as the tray of lamps and the light in everything as the One's light; Guru Nanak's aarti is also sung as kirtan in the evening.

chat.says: In Guru Nanak's aarti, is God out in the sky or inside people?
options: Both, in one hymn: the sky is the tray, and the light in everyone is the One's.
Out in the sky. The hymn praises the stars and leaves people out of it.
Inside people. The sky part is only there as a warning against nature.
